extracted.intended_audience: researchers and advanced graduate students in geometric analysis / Ricci flow (those studying Perelman’s surgery arguments)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and applies scale, curvature, volume, and surgery-control conditions (δ-cutoﬀs, r(t), canonical neighborhoods, admissible curves, reduced volume) used to deduce local curvature and noncollapsing conclusions for Ricci flow with surgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible and barely admissible space-time curves
rubrics_metrics.description: A space-time curve is called admissible if it stays in the region unaﬀected by surgery, and a space-time curve on the boundary of the set of admissible curves is called a barely admissible curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to restrict consideration to curves/geodesics that avoid surgery regions; minimal/geodesic connections that cross surgery regions are not admissible and therefore not minimal for the variational quantities (e.g., ¯L).

rubrics_metrics.name: Large Li–Yau–Perelman length for barely admissible curves (7.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For arbitrarily large L>0 one can find sufficiently small ¯δ(L,t0, r(t0), ε) > 0 so that whenever each δ-cutoﬀ in [tγ, t0] satisfies δ ≤ ¯δ(...) then any barely admissible curve γ parametrized by t with γ(t0)=x satisfies an integral lower bound of order L r0 (see (7.5.1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This estimate forces barely admissible curves to have very large Perelman-length when δ is sufficiently small, thereby ensuring minimizing curves avoid surgery collars; choice of ¯δ depends on L, t0, r(t0), ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability condition for Lemma 3.4.1 via ¯L bound
rubrics_metrics.description: If ¯L(y, τ) (the infimum Li–Yau length to (y,τ)) is achieved by admissible curves and satisfies ¯L(y, τ) ≤ 3√τ exp(C(A)+100), then Lemma 3.4.1(i) is applicable at that scale (with r0=1, t0=1 in the rescaled argument).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control of ¯L by an explicit bound ensures shortest geodesics from (x0,0) to (y,τ) lie in regions unaﬀected by surgery and allows differential inequalities for auxiliary functions (like h) to be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivity and differential inequality for cutoff function h
rubrics_metrics.description: Define h(y,t)=φ(d_t(x0,y)/(A(2t−1))) (¯L(y,τ) + 2√τ); then on the time-interval considered h is positive and (under admissibility of minimizing curves) satisfies a parabolic differential inequality of the form (∂/∂t − Δ)h ≥ −C(A) h + lower-order terms (see derivation around (7.5.2)–(7.5.4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing φ appropriately (rapidly increasing cutoff) and using ¯L bounds yields control on h's evolution; this is a technical device to obtain lower bounds on reduced volumes and control of minimizing curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perelman reduced-volume lower bound from volume noncollapsing (7.5.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Vol_{t0}(B_{t0}(x0,r0)) ≥ w r0^3 (and the parabolic neighborhood is unaﬀected by surgery and curvature scales are controlled), then Perelman's reduced volume Vr_{r0^2}^{-}(B_{t0−r0^2}(x0,r0)) has a positive lower bound c(A) (equation (7.5.8)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This uses scaling invariance of the Li–Yau–Perelman distance and is a key step toward obtaining a lower bound for Vol_{t0}(B_{t0}(x,ρ))/ρ^3; the constant depends only on A (the auxiliary parameter controlling cutoff φ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower bound for volume ratio (noncollapsing) of small balls
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the hypotheses that a cone-like set of shortest ℓ-geodesics from (x,t0) to B_{t0}(x0,r0) lies entirely in the unaﬀected region and previous reduced-volume estimates hold, there is a positive lower bound (depending only on A or w) for Vol_{t0}(B_{t0}(x,ρ))/ρ^3 for ρ at the appropriate scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine Perelman Jacobian comparison (Theorem 3.2.7), reduced-volume bound, and Gaussian-type estimates (see (7.5.9)–(7.5.12)) to deduce uniform noncollapsing at the microscopic scale ξρ^2; this is used repeatedly to prevent collapsing around points unaﬀected by surgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical neighborhood criterion for high curvature points (statement (ii)/(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: For sufficiently small δ-cutoﬀs (δ(t) nonincreasing and chosen small enough depending on A and time), any point with sufficiently large scalar curvature relative to the local scale must satisfy the canonical neighborhood statement (i.e., be an ε-neck, ε-cap, or have a canonical neighborhood modeled on an ancient κ-solution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof uses an induction/adjustment argument selecting a point (¯x,¯t) violating the statement, rescaling by its curvature, and deriving a contradiction by extracting an ancient κ-solution; thus the canonical neighborhood property is enforced by choosing δ small and using curvature/volume controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: δ(t) and r(t) are nonincreasing positive functions tied to surgery
rubrics_metrics.description: The surgery construction is assumed to be made with nonincreasing (continuous) positive functions δ(t) and r(t); each δ-cutoff at time t uses δ=δ(t) and the surgery cutoff radius h at a time interval is compared with scales r0 (see Theorem 7.5.2 hypotheses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monotonicity and smallness of δ(t) and the relation of r(t) to spatial scales are part of the hypothesis ensuring surgeries are controlled and estimates (canonical neighborhoods, curvature bounds) persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local curvature upper bound from volume and lower curvature control (Theorem 7.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ε>0 and w>0 there exist τ,K,¯r,θ,T so that if a solution (constructed as above) on [0,t0] satisfies: r0 ≤ r(t0), θ^{-1} h ≤ r0 ≤ ¯r√t0 (h maximal cutoff radius in [t0/2,t0]), and on B_{t0}(x0,r0) one has Rm(x,t0) ≥ − r0^{-2} and Vol_{t0}(B_{t0}(x0,r0)) ≥ w r0^3, then the solution is defined and satisfies R(x,t) < K r0^{-2} in the whole parabolic neighborhood P(x0,t0, τ r0^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the principal scale-invariant curvature control: a lower bound on Rm (no large negative curvature) plus a volume noncollapsing condition on the ball at time t0 force a two-sided curvature bound in a space-time neighborhood, provided r0 is within surgery/scale thresholds (θ,¯r,T).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pinching assumption (rewritten form)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pinching assumption can be rewritten as Rm ≥ −[f^{-1}(R(1+t))/(R(1+t))] R where f(x)=x(log x − 3) is increasing and convex; this controls negative part of curvature by scalar curvature function, and f^{-1}(y)/y → 0 as y→∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pinching relation is used to deduce nonnegativity controls under rescalings and to ensure limit solutions have nonnegative sectional curvature, enabling maximum principle and compactness arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a small ball with controlled positive volume inside any noncollapsed ball
rubrics_metrics.description: Given Vol_{t0}(B_{t0}(x0,r0)) ≥ w r0^3 and curvature lower bounds, one can find a subball B_{t0}(x',r') ⊂ B_{t0}(x0,r0) with r' comparable to r0 (r' ≥ ξ' r0) and Vol_{t0}(B_{t0}(x',r')) ≥ (1/2) α_3 (r')^3, i.e., nearly Euclidean volume at that smaller radius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This local almost-Euclidean ball is used to apply previous arguments (canonical neighborhood, curvature bounds) iteratively and to propagate estimates backward in time; constants ξ', α_3 depend only on the fixed volume parameter w.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backward extension / compactness via rescaling to ancient κ-solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting counterexample sequences (points where canonical neighborhood or curvature bounds fail), rescale by curvature at those points and shift time to obtain limits; if surgery parameters and volume/curvature controls hold, any limit must be an ancient κ-solution (contradiction unless the hypothesis is violated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a methodological criterion: failure of canonical neighborhood or curvature bounds at controlled scales leads (under assumed hypotheses) to a rescaled limit with bounded curvature and nonnegative sectional curvature, thereby excluding the failure by compactness and the strong maximum principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform κ-noncollapsing at controlled points
rubrics_metrics.description: From the volume and curvature lower bounds and previous estimates, one obtains uniform κ-noncollapsing at chosen base points (e.g., (¯x,¯t)); this provides injectivity/volume scale control necessary for Hamilton compactness arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: κ-noncollapsing plus local curvature bounds allow extraction of C^∞_loc limits and application of Hamilton’s compactness theorem to obtain ancients or contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iteration and backward propagation of curvature & volume estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a ball at time t0 with R bounded above by K' r0^{-2} on a forward/backward parabolic neighborhood and a volume lower bound, one can find earlier times t1 = t0 − τ'(r')^2 and subballs where similar curvature and volume bounds hold; repeating yields control down to the desired backward time slice (see the repeated derivation of (7.5.20)–(7.5.23)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This iterative scheme is used to extend local curvature control backward in time as long as surgery scales remain below the working radius and the pinching assumption holds; constants at each step depend only on previously fixed universal constants.
